title: What is a multi-account AWS strategy: separate accounts for dev/staging/prod (blast radius isolation), use AWS Organizations for centralized billing and policy, use SSO for access: and why is one big account for everything a bad idea (security risk, no isolation)?
shortTitle: Multi-Account AWS Strategy and Why One Big Account Is a Bad Idea
keyPoints: An AWS account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS provides; resources in separate accounts are fully isolated by default.
Separate accounts for dev, staging, and production contain blast radius so a mistake in development cannot touch production.
AWS Organizations provides consolidated billing, volume discounts, and Service Control Policies that set guardrails no account can override.
IAM Identity Center (SSO) gives single sign-on with role-based access into each account, centralizing onboarding and offboarding.
One big account is a bad idea because there is no isolation, shared service quotas, muddy cost attribution, and unlimited blast radius.
The management account should hold almost no workloads and be tightly guarded because it controls the entire organization.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use many AWS accounts to isolate blast radius, governed centrally by AWS Organizations with Service Control Policies and accessed through SSO, because one big account gives a mistake or breach unlimited reach across everything.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Multi-account strategy** – structuring a company's cloud into many AWS accounts (dev, staging, prod, per-team, per-workload) for strong blast-radius isolation, security, and billing separation.
- **AWS Organizations** – ties accounts together for consolidated billing, volume discounts, and Service Control Policies (guardrails that cap what any account can do).
- **IAM Identity Center (SSO)** – single sign-on with role-based access into permitted accounts, ideally federated from the corporate identity provider.
- **Service Control Policy (SCP)** – organization-wide guardrail that sets the maximum permissions any account can have; even account administrators cannot override it.
- **Management account** – the root account of the organization that should hold almost no workloads and be tightly guarded.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India kept all its money, customer records, training materials, and experiments in one single giant room with one door. A junior running an experiment could knock over the shelf holding real customer records. A multi-account strategy is having separate locked rooms -- a production vault, a staging practice vault, a development sandbox -- each with its own door and guard. Organizations is the head office that pays one combined bill and sets rules every room must follow. SSO is the single badge that opens only the specific rooms each employee is allowed into.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A multi-account AWS strategy structures an organization's cloud into many separate AWS accounts, because an account is the strongest isolation boundary AWS provides. The standard approach is at least separate accounts for development, staging, and production, plus dedicated accounts for logging, security, and shared services. The point is blast-radius isolation: because accounts are hard walls by default, a runaway script or leaked credential in development simply cannot reach the production ledger.

AWS Organizations is the governance layer that makes many accounts manageable. It gives consolidated billing with volume discounts, Service Control Policies that cap what any account can do (even administrators cannot override them), and Organizational Units for grouping and policy inheritance. IAM Identity Center provides single sign-on so users sign in once and assume only the roles and accounts they are entitled to.

Putting everything in one big account is a bad idea for concrete reasons: no blast-radius isolation, shared service quotas, muddy cost attribution, and a single breach exposing everything.

At National Bank of India I used a multi-account landing zone. Development, staging, and production were separate accounts. Organizations gave us consolidated billing and SCPs that made it impossible for any account to disable audit logging. SSO gave engineers access only to the accounts they needed. The management account held no workloads and was guarded tightly.

Remember one sentence: use separate AWS accounts for blast-radius isolation, govern them centrally with Organizations and SCPs, and access them through SSO -- because one big account gives a mistake or breach unlimited reach across everything.
